text:
Ontario Court (General Division)

Citation: Saleh v. Reichert

Court File: 74406/93

Date: 1993-06-07

Bell J.

Counsel:

John P. Telfer
,
for plaintiff.

Justin R. Fogarty
,
for defendant.

[
1
]

Bell
J.:—This sad case arises out of the death by accident on
May 7, 1993, of Layla Reichert, a young 27-year-old woman, who was brought up
in the Muslim faith. Her husband, Andreas Reichert, the defendant, seeks to
have his deceased wife's remains cremated, in accordance with what he perceives
were her expressed wishes. Her father, Kassem Saleh, the plaintiff, seeks to
prevent the cremation and seeks to have his daughter's remains disposed of by
burial because one of the fundamental tenets of the Muslim faith is that, if a
body is not somehow buried in the ground, it cannot be properly received by
God.

[
2
]

At a time when both her husband and her
father, as well as other members of her family and the community, are grieving
her loss, each wants to do what he perceives to be the right thing. It is
unfortunate that their views of what is right in the circumstances are
irreconcilable and it has been necessary to apply to this court for a legal
resolution of the issue.

[
3
]

On May 11, 1993, Houston J. granted an
ex
parte
motion by the plaintiff for an order enjoining the defendant from
cremating the remains or otherwise disposing of them other than by burial in
the ground. So that this matter might be dealt with expeditiously, the court
directed that it proceed to trial on May 28, 1993. The parties have co-operated
throughout. Affidavit evidence was filed on the original
ex parte
motion
and in anticipation of the hearing of the return of the plaintiff's motion and
the defendant's cross-motion. The parties have agreed that the affidavit
evidence would constitute the evidence at trial. Those affidavits were filed as
ex. 1 at trial. No issue was taken as to the admissibility of any of the
evidence although submissions have been made as to the weight to be accorded to
it.

[
4
]

The questions to be decided are on whom
the duty to dispose of the remains falls and what is the nature of the duty
imposed upon that person.

[
5
]

The evidence discloses that Layla
Reichert grew up in a Muslim household. She and Andreas Reichert were married
at the Ottawa mosque on April 14, 1988. Prior to his marriage to Layla
Reichert, Andreas Reichert converted to the Muslim faith. He was instructed in
the teachings of Islam by Tawfik Shaheen, the imam or minister of the Ottawa
mosque. Andreas Reichert stated in his affidavit that he agreed to convert to
the Muslim faith in order to facilitate his marriage to Layla Reichert and to
appease her family's opposition. He stated further that after their marriage he
and his wife never attended the mosque, nor did they observe Muslim rites or
rituals at any time. Tawfik Shaheen stated in his affidavit that Andreas
Reichert has now told him that he was only a Muslim for the time of the
marriage. Tawfik Shaheen stated further that, if he had known that he had been
deceived by Andreas Reichert as to whether he truly understood and believed the
faith of Islam, he would never have performed the marriage.

[
6
]

I accept the affidavit evidence of
Andreas Reichert and his mother, Erika Reichert, and his sister, Carol
Reichert, that, around February 14, 1993, Layla Reichert expressed to them an
abhorrence of burial and expressed the wish to be cremated in the event of her
death. I accept the affidavit evidence of Andreas Reichert that, at the
beginning of May, 1993, Layla Reichert expressed to him again her wish to be
cremated in the event of her death. Further, I accept the affidavit evidence of
Patricia Stoate, a coworker and friend of Layla Reichert, that, in a
conversation Patricia Stoate had with Layla Reichert during the past year,
Layla Reichert stated to her explicitly that she did not want to be buried, that
she wanted to be cremated.

[
7
]

Layla Reichert died on May 7, 1993,
without a will. Andreas Reichert was appointed as administrator of the estate
of Layla Reichert by letters of administration dated May 21, 1993. The evidence
to which I have referred about statements made by Layla Reichert to members of
Andreas Reichert's family and to a friend about her wish to be cremated
explains why Andreas Reichert has stated in his affidavit that he believes that
it is his duty as administrator to carry out Layla Reichert's expressed wishes.
Although I am satisfied that, prior to her death, Layla Reichert did express
the wish to be cremated, that is not dispositive of the issues before me, as an
expressed wish of a person directing the disposition of his or her body cannot
be enforced in law even if stated in a will or other instrument: see
Williams
v. Williams

(1882),
20 Ch. D. 659
at p. 665
.

[
8
]

It is not disputed that, upon the death
of a person, a duty arises to bury or otherwise dispose of the remains in a
decent and dignified fashion. The first issue to be determined is upon whom
that duty falls.

[
9
]

In
Hunter v. Hunter
,
1930 CanLII 357 (ON SCHCD)
,
[1930] 4
D.L.R. 255
,
65 O.L.R. 586 (H.C.)
, the deceased, who had been a Protestant,
expressed his desire to be buried in the place where his wife would be buried,
which would have been a Roman Catholic cemetery. He converted to Roman
Catholicism before his death. On his death, there was a contest between family
members as to where he should be buried.

[
10
]

At pp. 263-4, McEvoy J. stated:

The law as to who has the right to
the possession of a dead body for the purposes of burial, as distinguished from
the question of upon whom a duty of burial devolves, may not be entirely well
settled. In 3 Hals., p. 405, para. 851, it is stated: —

"The law as to the persons upon
whom the duty of disposing of a dead body falls, and as to the nature of that
duty, is imperfectly developed."

It is there said also that there is
authority for the propositions: (
a
) that the duty is incumbent upon the
executor; (
b
) on the husband of a deceased wife; (
c
) on the
parent of a deceased child; and (
d
) on any householder on whose premises
the body lies.

[
11
]

After reviewing the authorities, McEvoy
J. concluded that the executor, who was the deceased's son, had the right to
have the body for the purposes of burial over the competing claim by the widow.

[
12
]

In
Williams v. Williams, supra
, at
p. 664, Kay J. quoted with approval from
Williams on Executors
, 6th ed.,
p. 906, where it was said: "'It is now proposed to consider the duties of
an executor or administrator. And first, he must bury the deceased in a manner
suitable to the estate he leaves behind him.'" Kay J. went on to state:

It has been argued that this only
applies to the expenses of the burial; but I do not agree with that contention.
It means, and I understand the law of this country to be, that
prima facie

the executors are entitled to the possession and are responsible for the burial
of a dead body ...

[
13
]

In
Williams v. Williams
an
executor had been appointed but the quotation from
Williams on Executors

approved of by McKay J. refers to executors and administrators interchangeably.

[
14
]

In
Abeziz v. Harris Estate
,
[1992]
O.J. No. 1271
(Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)) [summarized
34 A.C.W.S. (3d) 360
], a
mother applied for an injunction restraining the cremation of her son. She was
Jewish and wished her son to have a proper Jewish burial even though he had
expressed his wish to be cremated. His executor, a lawyer, wanted to respect
and accede to his wish to be cremated. The central issue in that case related
to whether there were suspicious circumstances as to the two wills made by the
deceased in which reference was made to cremation. Thus, while the positions of
the parties in that case as to burial versus cremation arising out of religious
conviction were similar to the case before me, the central issue in that case
has no applicability to the facts before me. However, in the course of his judgment
Farley J. stated at p. 22:

As I read the cases and texts (
R.
v. Vann

(1851),
2 Den. 325
,
169 E.R. 523 (C.C.R.)
; Williams, Mortimer and
Sunnucks, pp. 66-7; A.H. Oosterhoff,
Text, Commentary and Cases on Wills and
Succession
, 3rd ed. (1990), p. 133, and 10 Hals., 4th ed., p. 486, para.
1017, "cremation and burial") I understand that there is no legal
right in a corpse (absent possibly some interim element under the
Anatomy
Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. A.21, for medical research). Rather than rights there
are only obligations. This is an obligation the law places on the executor if
there is one. The fundamental obligation is that the body be appropriately
dealt with — that is disposed of in a dignified fashion. Burial and cremation
come to mind as being specifically sanctioned in Ontario. I appreciate that
Orthodox Judaism prohibits cremation but Aida's counsel, without prompting,
voluntarily advised that religious law had no bearing in this hearing. While
one cannot be human if one were to ignore the distress Aida has in the
circumstances, it does not seem to me that in the legal sense any of her rights
are being affected. Rather she is being relieved of a legal obligation of Ben's
body, an obligation that would fall to her as parent pursuant to
Vann.
(I
do appreciate that she would gladly bear this obligation.) Ben's executrix Jane
does have the legal obligation to attend to this using estate funds.

[
15
]

After considering the authorities to
which I have referred, I conclude that, in the circumstances before me, the duty
to dispose of the remains of Layla Reichert would fall upon Andreas Reichert as
the administrator of his deceased wife's estate and that Andreas Reichert would
have the right to have the remains for the purpose of disposing of them.

[
16
]

In his argument, counsel for the
plaintiff, Kassem Saleh, questioned the validity of the marriage of Layla and
Andreas Reichert. He pointed out that Andreas Reichert's right to
administration of the estate of Layla Reichert was based on his marriage to
Layla Reichert. Further, he submitted that there was clear evidence that the
marriage was solemnized by deceit of the imam, who would not have performed it
if he had known that the defendant was not a Muslim. He submitted that would
have rendered the marriage void although he added that he was not asking me to
void the marriage as it had now been ended by the death of Layla Reichert.

[
17
]

At its highest, counsel for the
plaintiff was submitting that this would have been a voidable marriage. The
validity of a voidable marriage can only be determined in proceedings for a
nullity decree brought by one of the parties to the marriage and, thus, a
voidable marriage cannot be challenged after the marriage has been ended by the
death of one of the parties: see Hovius,
Family Law
, 2nd ed. (1987), at
pp. 93-4. There was no evidence before me to suggest that this was not a good
marriage and there was no evidence that any application had been made during
the lifetime of Layla Reichert for a nullity decree. Accordingly, no basis has
been raised upon which the plaintiff could challenge the validity of the
marriage and the grant of letters of administration to Andreas Reichert.

[
18
]

Having determined upon whom the duty
falls, the second issue to be determined is the nature of the duty imposed on
the administrator, Andreas Reichert. The old common law cases referred to the
duty as being a duty to provide a "decent Christian burial". That has
been modified with the times. In
R. v. Price

(1884),
12 Q.B.D. 247
,
Stephen J. held that the term "Christian burial" as used was
obviously inapplicable to persons who were not Christians. Cremation is now
recognized under the
Cemeteries Act (Revised)
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.4, as
being a method of disposal of human remains so that, by 1992 when Farley J.
decided
Abeziz, supra
, he stated, as I have noted earlier, that the
fundamental obligation is that the body be disposed of in a dignified fashion.
He noted that burial and cremation came to mind as being specifically
sanctioned in Ontario.

[
19
]

Counsel for the plaintiff, Kassem Saleh,
acknowledged that both burial and cremation could be dignified methods of
disposal of a body, but, he submitted, not in every situation. He argued that
it would depend on the circumstances. In considering the nature of the common
law duty to be imposed, counsel for the plaintiff asked me to consider the
wisdom shown in a general reading of the ancient common law cases as opposed
simply to considering specific principles enunciated. I shall deal with this
submission after I have dealt with the other specific submissions made by
counsel for the plaintiff.

[
20
]

Counsel for the plaintiff also asked me
to consider the spirit and purpose of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
, particularly the preamble's reference to Canada being founded
upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law and the
reference in s. 27 to interpretation in a manner consistent with the
preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians. I
accept the submissions of counsel for the defendant, Andreas Reichert, that the
Charter does not, in the absence of state or governmental action, apply to
private parties involved in litigation: see
R.W.D.U., Local 580 v. Dolphin
Delivery Ltd.

(1986),
1986 CanLII 5 (SCC)
,
33 D.L.R. (4th) 174
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 573
,
38 C.C.L.T.
184
, and
Tremblay v. Daigle

(1989),
1989 CanLII 33 (SCC)
,
62 D.L.R. (4th) 634
,
[1989] 2 S.C.R.
530
, 11 C.H.R.R. D/165.

[
21
]

Counsel for the plaintiff, Kassem
Saleh, also submitted that, by his acts, Andreas Reichert had undertaken what
the nature of the duty would be. Counsel for the plaintiff referred to Andreas
Reichert's act of conversion to the Muslim faith. The document signed by
Andreas Reichert, at the time of his conversion in March, 1987, is attached as
ex. "B" to the affidavit of Tawfik Shaheen sworn May 11, 1993. In it
Andreas Reichert pledged to God that he would live up to the standards of Islam
obeying its orders and evading its prohibitions.

[
22
]

Counsel for the plaintiff submitted as
well that, by the further act of entering into marriage with Layla Reichert as
a person of Muslim faith, Andreas Reichert undertook to carry out his duties as
a husband such that any obligation falling to him upon her death now required
that he carry out that obligation or trust upon terms reasonably consistent
with, and not unreasonably offensive to, the orders and prohibitions of the
Muslim faith, one of which prohibits cremation because, if the body is
destroyed rather than buried in the ground, it cannot properly be received by
God. Counsel for the plaintiff submitted that this was an undertaking, express
or implied, which, when translated into English law, is an undertaking the
breach of which would be the breach of a duty to bury.

[
23
]

I accept the submission of counsel for
the defendant, Andreas Reichert, that what Andreas Reichert signed on his conversion
was a statement of conscience. It was a pledge to God. It is not enforceable by
Kassem Saleh in a civil action.

[
24
]

I see no merit in this civil case in
the arguments raised by counsel for the plaintiff arising out of the provisions
of
s. 182
of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, relating to the
neglect of any duty imposed or undertaken to bury a dead person and relating to
improper or indecent interference with a dead person's body or remains.

[
25
]

I return then to the submission of
counsel for the plaintiff, Kassem Saleh, that I consider the circumstances and
the wisdom shown in the common law cases as they have developed. I should state
that, in view of counsel's submissions, I have perused the authorities put
before me by counsel rather than going simply to the specific principles in the
cases referred to by counsel. Having done so, I have concluded simply that the
fundamental duty or obligation is that the remains be disposed of in a decent
and dignified fashion. Further, as burial and cremation are both specifically
sanctioned in Ontario, disposal by either means would meet the requirement for
disposal in a decent and dignified fashion. The
Abeziz
case,
supra
,
was decided by Farley J. on the understanding that religious law had no bearing
on the case. I have concluded that is the situation here as well. I agree with
Farley J.'s view, as he expressed it at p. 23, that there are only legal
obligations. I also conclude, as did Farley J. in the case before him, that, in
the legal sense, none of the rights of the plaintiff, Kassem Saleh, as a parent
are being affected.

[
26
]

Counsel for the plaintiff also
submitted that an order should be granted estopping the defendant from
cremating Layla Reichert's remains. I find nothing in the circumstances of this
case which would justify the granting of such an order.

[
27
]

As the plaintiff has not proved his
case, his action is dismissed. As requested by the defendant, order to go:
setting aside the
ex parte
order for injunction of Houston J. dated May
11, 1993; declaring that Andreas Reichert, as administrator of the estate of
Layla Reichert, has the sole right to determine how to dispose of the last
remains of Layla Reichert, and declaring that the last remains of Layla
Reichert may be disposed of by burial or cremation. As I stated earlier in this
judgment, the expressed wishes of a person as to the disposition of his or her
body cannot be enforced in law. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent an
executor or administrator, on whom the duty falls to dispose of the remains,
from carrying out the deceased's lawful wishes concerning the disposal of his
or her body: see
Abeziz
at p. 20. Accordingly, Andreas Reichert, as
administrator, may carry out the wishes which Layla Reichert expressed to him,
to his family members and to her friend, Patricia Stoate, with respect to
cremation, if he so chooses.

[
28
]

Both counsel indicated that this was
not a case for costs to be awarded. As I complete this difficult judgment which
has had to be rendered in circumstances which are so sad and yet so intensely
meaningful to both parties, I want to recognize and commend both counsel and
their clients for the way this case has been conducted so as to respect the
sensibilities of each side to the greatest extent possible.

[
29
]

Action dismissed.
